claim: Neutrophils started to migrate and accumulate in the peritoneal cavity within 4 hr after IL-1β injection in WT mice.
source: In WT mice, neutrophils started to migrate and accumulate in the peritoneal cavity within 4 hr after IL-1β injection (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing absolute number of Ly6G+ cells in peritoneal cavity over time (Figure 1A).

claim: In Pecam1-/- mice, neutrophils started to migrate to the peritoneal cavity during the first 2 hr, but eventually failed to extravasate within the peritoneal fluid at later time points.
source: However, in Pecam1-/- mice, neutrophils started to migrate to the peritoneal cavity during the first 2 hr, but eventually failed to extravasate within the peritoneal fluid at later time points (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced neutrophil accumulation in Pecam1-/- mice at 4 hr compared to WT (Figure 1A).

claim: There was no defective molecular response to IL-1β in Pecam1-/- mice in terms of chemokines involved in neutrophil mobilization from the bone marrow (SDF-1), local endothelial/platelet activation at sites of extravasation (P-selectin), specific chemoattraction at the inflammatory site (CXCL1), or global acute-phase reaction (PTX3).
source: nor was there a defective molecular response to IL-1β in terms of chemokines involved in neutrophil mobilization from the bone marrow (SDF-1), local endothelial/platelet activation at sites of extravasation (P-selectin), specific chemoattraction at the inflammatory site (CXCL1), or global acute-phase reaction (PTX3) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by measurements of SDF-1, CD62P, CXCL1, and PTX-3 concentrations showing no significant differences between WT and Pecam1-/- mice (Figure 1C).

claim: Neutrophils from WT mice were located within the extravascular space in the omentum.
source: Neutrophils from WT mice were located within the extravascular space (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images of whole-mount omentum showing Ly6G+ cells in extravascular space (Figure 1D).

claim: The phosphorylation level of CD31 (pY713) was inversely correlated with neutrophil distance from the vessel wall.
source: Notably, the phosphorylation level of CD31 (pY713) was inversely correlated with neutrophil distance from the vessel wall (i.e., increased pY713 when cells were close to the blood vessel wall), suggesting that CD31 signaling in neutrophils was active during extravasation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis showing inverse correlation between pY713 staining intensity and distance from vessel (Figure 1E).

claim: CD31 signaling in neutrophils was active during extravasation.
source: Notably, the phosphorylation level of CD31 (pY713) was inversely correlated with neutrophil distance from the vessel wall (i.e., increased pY713 when cells were close to the blood vessel wall), suggesting that CD31 signaling in neutrophils was active during extravasation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 phosphorylation (pY713) is highest when neutrophils are close to the vessel wall during extravasation (Figure 1E).

claim: Most neutrophils from Pecam1-/- mice were found to extravasate.
source: Although most neutrophils from Pecam1-/- mice were also found to extravasate (Figure 1F, inset 3D section), their migration was delayed as they remained in close contact with the outer layer of the vessel wall (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing Ly6G+ cells outside vessels in Pecam1-/- mice (Figure 1F).

claim: The migration of neutrophils from Pecam1-/- mice was delayed as they remained in close contact with the outer layer of the vessel wall.
source: Although most neutrophils from Pecam1-/- mice were also found to extravasate (Figure 1F, inset 3D section), their migration was delayed as they remained in close contact with the outer layer of the vessel wall (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: Supported by quantification showing significantly shorter distance of Pecam1-/- neutrophils from vessels compared to WT (Figure 1F-H).

claim: CD31 is involved in facilitating the detachment of neutrophils from the outer components of the vessel wall after extravasation.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that CD31 is involved in facilitating the detachment of neutrophils from the outer components of the vessel wall after extravasation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Pecam1-/- neutrophils remain attached to the outer vessel wall while WT neutrophils detach and migrate away (Figure 1F-H).

claim: Detachment from the outer vessel wall is crucial for the timely migration of neutrophils to the inflammatory site.
source: This detachment is crucial for the timely migration to the inflammatory site.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Pecam1-/- neutrophils fail to reach the inflammatory site in a timely manner due to their inability to detach from the vessel wall (Figure 1A, 1F-H).

claim: 173 proteins were co-immunoprecipitated with CD31 molecules in human neutrophils.
source: We identified 173 protein co-immunoprecipitated with CD31 molecules (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis using Orbitrap mass spectrometry of CD31 immunoprecipitates (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).

claim: 110 proteins were present in both resting and fMLP-stimulated conditions in the CD31 interactome.
source: A total of 110 proteins were present in both resting and fMLP-stimulated conditions, whereas 43 proteins were only associated with CD31 molecules under resting conditions and 20 proteins were specifically detected under fMLP stimulation (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis of proteomic data (Figure 2B).

claim: 43 proteins were only associated with CD31 molecules under resting conditions.
source: A total of 110 proteins were present in both resting and fMLP-stimulated conditions, whereas 43 proteins were only associated with CD31 molecules under resting conditions and 20 proteins were specifically detected under fMLP stimulation (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis of proteomic data (Figure 2B).

claim: 20 proteins were specifically detected under fMLP stimulation in the CD31 interactome.
source: A total of 110 proteins were present in both resting and fMLP-stimulated conditions, whereas 43 proteins were only associated with CD31 molecules under resting conditions and 20 proteins were specifically detected under fMLP stimulation (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis of proteomic data (Figure 2B).

claim: Known CD31-interacting proteins in chemokine-stimulated neutrophils include GRB2, CD177, SHP, and MSN.
source: Among these, we found known CD31-interacting proteins in chemokine-stimulated neutrophils, such as GRB2, CD177, SHP, and MSN (Sachs et al., 2007), as well as ITIM-interacting SH2 phosphatase SHIP1 (Pumphrey et al., 1999), and integrins such as CD11b and CD18 (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data and cited previous studies (Sachs et al., 2007) (Figure 2C).

claim: SHIP1 is an ITIM-interacting SH2 phosphatase that associates with CD31.
source: Among these, we found known CD31-interacting proteins in chemokine-stimulated neutrophils, such as GRB2, CD177, SHP, and MSN (Sachs et al., 2007), as well as ITIM-interacting SH2 phosphatase SHIP1 (Pumphrey et al., 1999), and integrins such as CD11b and CD18 (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data and cited previous study (Pumphrey et al., 1999) (Figure 2C).

claim: Integrins such as CD11b and CD18 associate with CD31.
source: Among these, we found known CD31-interacting proteins in chemokine-stimulated neutrophils, such as GRB2, CD177, SHP, and MSN (Sachs et al., 2007), as well as ITIM-interacting SH2 phosphatase SHIP1 (Pumphrey et al., 1999), and integrins such as CD11b and CD18 (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data showing CD11b and CD18 in CD31 immunoprecipitates (Figure 2C).

claim: The CD31 interactome was linked to the integrin and actin networks, under resting and activated conditions.
source: Ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) and KEGG functional annotation pathways revealed that the CD31 interactome was linked to the integrin and actin networks, under resting and activated conditions, consistent with the role of CD31 in neutrophil migration (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by IPA and KEGG pathway analysis of proteomic data (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).

claim: CD31, through SHIP1 (INDPP5), regulates cytoskeleton reorganization and integrin activation during neutrophil migration.
source: Based on the IPA results, we elaborated a model of protein interaction showing how CD31, through SHIP1 (INDPP5), regulates cytoskeleton reorganization and integrin activation during neutrophil migration (Figure 2E).
evidence: Inferred from IPA network analysis of CD31 interactome showing connections between CD31, SHIP1, and cytoskeletal/integrin proteins (Figure 2E).

claim: Both CD31 and CD11b rapidly relocated to the uropod during neutrophil migration.
source: We found that both CD31 and CD11b rapidly relocated to the uropod during neutrophil migration (Figure 2F and G and Video 1), while a minor fraction of both molecules remained localized at the leading edge.
evidence: Supported by live imaging microscopy showing CD31 and CD11b localization at the uropod (Figure 2F and G and Video 1).

claim: A minor fraction of CD31 and CD11b remained localized at the leading edge during neutrophil migration.
source: We found that both CD31 and CD11b rapidly relocated to the uropod during neutrophil migration (Figure 2F and G and Video 1), while a minor fraction of both molecules remained localized at the leading edge.
evidence: Supported by live imaging microscopy showing some CD31 and CD11b at the leading edge (Figure 2F and G).

claim: CD31 localizes preferentially to the uropod in human neutrophils interacting with immobilized ICAM-1 and IL-8.
source: Under these conditions, we found that CD31 localizes preferentially to the uropod and, only at the rear, CD31 displayed phosphorylated ITIM motifs (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing CD31 localization at the uropod (Figure 2H).

claim: Only at the rear of neutrophils, CD31 displayed phosphorylated ITIM motifs.
source: Under these conditions, we found that CD31 localizes preferentially to the uropod and, only at the rear, CD31 displayed phosphorylated ITIM motifs (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing pY713 staining at the uropod (Figure 2H).

claim: SHIP1 was concentrated at the cellular rear of migrating neutrophils.
source: In addition, SH2-containing inositol phosphatase SHIP1, which has been found in the CD31 interactome, was also concentrated at the cellular rear (Figure 2I), supporting the notion that functional CD31 molecular clusters are present in the uropods of motile neutrophils.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing SHIP-1 localization at the uropod (Figure 2I).

claim: Functional CD31 molecular clusters are present in the uropods of motile neutrophils.
source: In addition, SH2-containing inositol phosphatase SHIP1, which has been found in the CD31 interactome, was also concentrated at the cellular rear (Figure 2I), supporting the notion that functional CD31 molecular clusters are present in the uropods of motile neutrophils.
evidence: Inferred from the co-localization of CD31, phosphorylated CD31 (pY713), and SHIP1 at the uropod (Figure 2H, 2I).

claim: Clusters positive for NKI-L16 (indicating active integrins) were exclusively localized at the leading edge, where CD31 was absent.
source: Clusters positive for NKI-L16 (indicating active integrins, shown in red) were exclusively localized at the leading edge, where CD31 (shown in green) was absent.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing mutually exclusive distribution of NKI-L16 and CD31 (Figure 2J).

claim: The staining with NKI-L16 antibody was absent at the uropod, where most CD31 was concentrated.
source: Conversely, the staining with this antibody was absent at the uropod, where most CD31 was concentrated (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing absence of NKI-L16 staining at the uropod where CD31 is concentrated (Figure 2J).

claim: CD31 is enriched at the uropod along with closed β2-integrins, in contrast to fully opened integrins that are restricted to the leading edge.
source: The co-localization of functional CD31 clusters with integrins that did not react with the NKI-L16 antibody indicates that CD31 is enriched at the uropod along with closed β2-integrins, in contrast to fully opened integrins that are restricted to the leading edge.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 co-localizes with total CD11a but not with NKI-L16-positive (active) CD11a at the uropod (Figure 2J).

claim: CD31 signaling may contribute to maintaining integrins in a closed/bent conformation at the uropod during neutrophil migration.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that CD31 signaling may contribute to maintaining integrins in a closed/bent conformation at the uropod, the region where cell detachment is required, during neutrophil migration.
evidence: Inferred from the co-localization of CD31 with closed integrins at the uropod and the absence of active integrins in this region (Figure 2J).

claim: Wild-type neutrophils quickly polarized with a leading-edge rich in F-actin, while the integrin-associated protein talin accumulated at the uropod.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Pouwels et al., 2013), wild-type neutrophils quickly polarized with a leading-edge rich in F-actin, while the integrin-associated protein talin accumulated at the uropod, where the location of the two proteins was almost mutually exclusive (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification showing F-actin at the front and talin at the back of WT neutrophils (Figure 3A and B).

claim: The location of F-actin and talin was almost mutually exclusive in wild-type neutrophils.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Pouwels et al., 2013), wild-type neutrophils quickly polarized with a leading-edge rich in F-actin, while the integrin-associated protein talin accumulated at the uropod, where the location of the two proteins was almost mutually exclusive (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing spatial separation of F-actin and talin in WT neutrophils (Figure 3A and B).

claim: Talin was spatially far from F-actin at the cell rear in WT leukocytes, indicating that the integrins at the uropod were in a low-adhesive conformation state.
source: The fact that talin was spatially far from F-actin at the cell rear indicated that the integrins at the uropod of WT leukocytes were in a low-adhesive conformation state.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that talin and F-actin are spatially separated at the uropod, and talin is known to bridge cytoskeleton and active integrins (Figure 3A and B).

claim: Polarization was clearly defective in Pecam1-/- neutrophils, where F-actin was concentrated along with talin also at the cellular rear.
source: Instead, such polarization was clearly defective in Pecam1-/- neutrophils, where F-actin was concentrated along with talin also at the cellular rear (Figure 3C) so that Pecam1-/- neutrophils appeared particularly stretched and displayed more elongated uropods compared to wild-type cells (Figure 3D and E), thus reflecting an abnormal subcellular organization in the absence of CD31.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification showing co-localization of F-actin and talin at the rear of Pecam1-/- neutrophils (Figure 3C).

claim: Pecam1-/- neutrophils appeared particularly stretched and displayed more elongated uropods compared to wild-type cells.
source: Instead, such polarization was clearly defective in Pecam1-/- neutrophils, where F-actin was concentrated along with talin also at the cellular rear (Figure 3C) so that Pecam1-/- neutrophils appeared particularly stretched and displayed more elongated uropods compared to wild-type cells (Figure 3D and E), thus reflecting an abnormal subcellular organization in the absence of CD31.
evidence: Supported by quantification showing significantly longer uropods and larger cell area in Pecam1-/- neutrophils compared to WT (Figure 3D and E).

claim: Pecam1-/- neutrophils reflect an abnormal subcellular organization in the absence of CD31.
source: Instead, such polarization was clearly defective in Pecam1-/- neutrophils, where F-actin was concentrated along with talin also at the cellular rear (Figure 3C) so that Pecam1-/- neutrophils appeared particularly stretched and displayed more elongated uropods compared to wild-type cells (Figure 3D and E), thus reflecting an abnormal subcellular organization in the absence of CD31.
evidence: Inferred from the defective polarization, elongated uropods, and abnormal distribution of F-actin and talin in Pecam1-/- neutrophils (Figure 3C-E).

claim: In wild-type neutrophils, SHIP1 was preferentially localized together with CD44 at the site of a clearly identifiable uropod.
source: Whereas in wild-type neutrophils SHIP1 was preferentially localized together with CD44 at the site of a clearly identifiable uropod (Figure 3F), CD44 and SHIP1 were both distributed more evenly throughout the cell body in Pecam1-/- neutrophils.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing co-localization of SHIP1 and CD44 at the uropod in WT neutrophils (Figure 3F).

claim: CD44 and SHIP1 were both distributed more evenly throughout the cell body in Pecam1-/- neutrophils.
source: Whereas in wild-type neutrophils SHIP1 was preferentially localized together with CD44 at the site of a clearly identifiable uropod (Figure 3F), CD44 and SHIP1 were both distributed more evenly throughout the cell body in Pecam1-/- neutrophils.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing diffuse distribution of SHIP1 and CD44 in Pecam1-/- neutrophils (Figure 3G).

claim: CD31 was critically involved in uropod formation of neutrophils interacting with laminin.
source: These findings further supported the hypothesis that CD31 was critically involved in uropod formation of neutrophils interacting with laminin.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Pecam1-/- neutrophils show defective uropod formation and abnormal distribution of uropod markers (Figure 3F-G).

claim: Experiments performed with Pecam1ITIM-/- mice phenocopied the data obtained using whole Pecam1-/- deficiency.
source: Experiments performed with these mice phenocopied the data obtained using whole Pecam1-/- deficiency (Figure 3H–K), demonstrating that CD31 signaling properties are mandatory for proper polarization of migrating neutrophils.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification showing similar defects in Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils as in Pecam1-/- neutrophils (Figure 3H-K).

claim: CD31 signaling properties are mandatory for proper polarization of migrating neutrophils.
source: Experiments performed with these mice phenocopied the data obtained using whole Pecam1-/- deficiency (Figure 3H–K), demonstrating that CD31 signaling properties are mandatory for proper polarization of migrating neutrophils.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that deletion of CD31 ITIM motifs produces the same phenotype as complete CD31 deletion (Figure 3H-K).

claim: The CD31 agonist P8RI effectively rescued and sustained the functionality of CD31 ITIM in T lymphocytes.
source: In our previous studies, we demonstrated that P8RI, a CD31 agonist peptide, effectively rescued and sustained the functionality of CD31 ITIM in T lymphocytes (Clement et al., 2015; Fornasa et al., 2012; Fornasa et al., 2010) and macrophages (Andreata et al., 2018), thereby providing promising potential for theranostic applications (Hoang et al., 2018; Vigne et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Clement et al., 2015; Fornasa et al., 2012; Fornasa et al., 2010).

claim: The CD31 agonist P8RI effectively rescued and sustained the functionality of CD31 ITIM in macrophages.
source: In our previous studies, we demonstrated that P8RI, a CD31 agonist peptide, effectively rescued and sustained the functionality of CD31 ITIM in T lymphocytes (Clement et al., 2015; Fornasa et al., 2012; Fornasa et al., 2010) and macrophages (Andreata et al., 2018), thereby providing promising potential for theranostic applications (Hoang et al., 2018; Vigne et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Andreata et al., 2018).

claim: The CD31 agonist consistently sustained CD31 phosphorylation during fMLP activation in neutrophils.
source: In the context of neutrophils, we found that the CD31 agonist consistently sustained CD31 phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and clustering (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) during fMLP activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), specifically targeting the CD31 molecule (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and fine-tuning cytoskeleton dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot showing increased CD31 pY713 with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The CD31 agonist consistently sustained CD31 clustering during fMLP activation in neutrophils.
source: In the context of neutrophils, we found that the CD31 agonist consistently sustained CD31 phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and clustering (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) during fMLP activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), specifically targeting the CD31 molecule (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and fine-tuning cytoskeleton dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy showing increased CD31 clustering with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The CD31 agonist specifically targets the CD31 molecule in neutrophils.
source: In the context of neutrophils, we found that the CD31 agonist consistently sustained CD31 phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and clustering (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) during fMLP activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), specifically targeting the CD31 molecule (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and fine-tuning cytoskeleton dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry showing CD31 agonist binding only to WT but not Pecam1-/- neutrophils (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claim: The CD31 agonist fine-tunes cytoskeleton dynamics in neutrophils.
source: In the context of neutrophils, we found that the CD31 agonist consistently sustained CD31 phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and clustering (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) during fMLP activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), specifically targeting the CD31 molecule (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and fine-tuning cytoskeleton dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry showing altered actin polymerization kinetics with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).

claim: 1 hr after intradermal IL-1β injection, Lyz2-GFP+ cells exhibited crawling behavior along the post-capillary blood vessels.
source: Our observations revealed that 1 hr after intradermal IL-1β injection, Lyz2-GFP+ cells exhibited crawling behavior along the post-capillary blood vessels.
evidence: Supported by two-photon microscopy observations of Lyz2-GFP+ cells in vivo (Figure 4A).

claim: Extravasating leukocytes demonstrated delayed uropod detachment and underwent significant elongation before being disconnected from the basement membrane.
source: Extravasating leukocytes demonstrated delayed uropod detachment and underwent significant elongation before being disconnected from the basement membrane (Figure 4A and B and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by two-photon microscopy images showing elongated cells during extravasation (Figure 4A and B and Video 2).

claim: Administration of the CD31 agonist 1 hr after the initiation of Lyz2-GFP+ cell extravasation resulted in a remarkable acceleration of uropod detachment from the basement membrane.
source: Administration of the CD31 agonist 1 hr after the initiation of Lyz2-GFP+ cell extravasation resulted in a remarkable acceleration of uropod detachment from the basement membrane.
evidence: Supported by quantification showing significantly faster detachment speed with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4C).

claim: The CD31 agonist led to an increased migratory capacity of Lyz2-GFP+ cells in the extravascular space compared to cells from vehicle-treated mice.
source: This led to an increased migratory capacity of Lyz2-GFP+ cells in the extravascular space compared to cells from vehicle-treated mice (Figure 4A and B and Video 3).
evidence: Supported by two-photon microscopy images and quantification showing increased migration with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4A-C).

claim: The CD31 agonist enhanced the migratory capacity of extravasated Lyz2-GFP+ cells 3 hr after inducing inflammation in the extravascular space.
source: Furthermore, our investigation of the fate of extravasated Lyz2-GFP+ cells 3 hr after inducing inflammation revealed that the CD31 agonist enhanced their migratory capacity in the extravascular space (Figure 4C and D and Videos 4 and 5).
evidence: Supported by two-photon microscopy images and quantification showing enhanced migration at 3 hr with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4C-H).

claim: The CD31 agonist enhanced neutrophil migration as demonstrated by increased speed, shorter cellular length, and greater traveling distance compared to the control group.
source: This enhancement was demonstrated by increased speed, shorter cellular length, and greater traveling distance compared to the control group (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Supported by quantification of speed, length, circularity, and track plots showing enhanced migration with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 4E-H).

claim: CD31 signaling actively participates in uropod detachment from the vessel after neutrophil transendothelial migration outside the vessel wall.
source: Taken together, these gain-of-function experiments provided further evidence that CD31 signaling actively participates in uropod detachment from the vessel after neutrophil transendothelial migration outside the vessel wall.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that enhancing CD31 signaling with the agonist accelerates uropod detachment and improves migration (Figure 4A-H).

claim: In WT mice, RGD peptides did not modify IL-1β-induced neutrophil accumulation in the peritoneal cavity.
source: In WT mice, RGD peptides did not modify IL-1β-induced neutrophil accumulation in the peritoneal cavity (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing no significant difference in neutrophil numbers with RGD treatment in WT mice (Figure 5B and C).

claim: Extravascular (i.p.) injection of RGD peptides rescued the defective neutrophil accumulation in Pecam1-/- mice upon IL-1β-induced peritonitis.
source: However, extravascular (i.p.) injection of RGD peptides rescued the defective neutrophil accumulation in Pecam1-/- mice upon IL-1β-induced peritonitis (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing increased neutrophil numbers with RGD treatment in Pecam1-/- mice (Figure 5B and C).

claim: RGD injection enhanced extravascular detachment of Pecam1-/- neutrophils.
source: Corresponding fluorescent microscopy analysis confirmed the enhanced extravascular detachment of Pecam1-/- neutrophils upon RGD injection (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification showing increased distance of Pecam1-/- neutrophils from vessels with RGD treatment (Figure 5D and E).

claim: The CD31 agonist increased neutrophil recruitment into the peritoneal cavity.
source: Based on the observation that the CD31 agonist increased neutrophil recruitment into the peritoneal cavity (Figure 5F–H), we investigated whether CD31 intracellular signaling, rather than its ectodomain properties, plays a role in regulating the recruitment of neutrophils to the site of inflammation.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing increased neutrophil numbers with CD31 agonist treatment (Figure 5F-H).

claim: Despite equal frequencies of WT and Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils in the blood before and after IL-1β injection, Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils exhibited a disadvantage in recruitment into the inflamed peritoneum compared to their WT counterparts.
source: Despite equal frequencies of WT and Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils (identified by flow cytometry as CD45+ Ly6G+) in the blood before and after IL-1β injection (Figure 5J and K), Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils exhibited a disadvantage in recruitment into the inflamed peritoneum compared to their WT counterparts.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing equal frequencies in blood but reduced recruitment of Pecam1ITIM-/- neutrophils to peritoneum (Figure 5J-L).

claim: The CD31 ITIM-dependent intracellular pathway plays a pivotal role in regulating neutrophil migration within the extravascular space during inflammation.
source: In summary, our collective findings provide compelling evidence that the CD31 ITIM-dependent intracellular pathway plays a pivotal role in regulating neutrophil migration within the extravascular space during inflammation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that deletion of CD31 ITIM motifs impairs neutrophil recruitment to inflammatory sites (Figure 5I-L).

claim: CD31 ITIM-dependent pathway effectively controls integrin activation at the uropod.
source: Specifically, it effectively controls integrin activation at the uropod, thereby exerting a significant influence on the efficient movement of neutrophils.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 co-localizes with closed integrins at the uropod and its absence leads to defective uropod detachment (Figure 2J, Figure 3, Figure 5).

claim: CD31 regulatory mechanism ensures the timely arrival of neutrophils at the inflammatory site, facilitating their efficient migration and precise targeting of the inflamed area.
source: This regulatory mechanism ensures the timely arrival of neutrophils at the inflammatory site, facilitating their efficient migration and precise targeting of the inflamed area, thereby optimizing the immune response.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 deficiency or ITIM deletion delays neutrophil arrival at inflammatory sites (Figure 1, Figure 5).

claim: CD31 signaling at the uropod plays a key role in the polarization and detachment of neutrophils.
source: We found that CD31 signaling at the uropod plays a key role in the polarization and detachment of neutrophils, which is crucial for initiating their migration within the vascular compartment and subsequent progression through the interstitial tissue following extravasation towards inflammatory sites.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 localizes to the uropod, its absence causes defective polarization and detachment, and enhancing its signaling improves these processes (Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 4).

claim: The uropod remains trapped at the basolateral membrane of endothelial cell junctions, while the leading edge moves forward in the interstitial tissue.
source: Our observations confirmed the dynamic behavior of neutrophils, wherein the uropod remains trapped at the basolateral membrane of endothelial cell junctions, while the leading edge moves forward in the interstitial tissue (Hind et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Hind et al., 2016) and confirmed by observations in this study.

claim: The detachment of the uropod is a crucial process that enables neutrophils to transition from a firmly adhesive state within blood vessels to a rapidly migratory configuration in the static extravascular space.
source: The detachment of the uropod is a crucial process that enables neutrophils to transition from a firmly adhesive state within blood vessels, under strong hemodynamic conditions, to a rapidly migratory configuration in the static extravascular space.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that neutrophils must detach from the vessel wall to migrate effectively in the extravascular space (Figure 1, Figure 4).

claim: The administration of soluble RGD peptides in the extravascular space effectively rescued the stagnation of Pecam1-/- neutrophils within the extracellular matrix.
source: Nevertheless, our data unequivocally demonstrated that the administration of soluble RGD peptides in the extravascular space effectively rescued the stagnation of Pecam1-/- neutrophils within the extracellular matrix.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and microscopy data showing increased neutrophil detachment and recruitment with RGD treatment in Pecam1-/- mice (Figure 5B-E).

claim: RGD peptides competitively bind to the RDG motif found in various extracellular matrix proteins, potentially reversing the excessive adhesion of RGD-binding β1 integrins.
source: These peptides competitively bind to the RDG motif found in various extracellular matrix proteins, potentially reversing the excessive adhesion of RGD-binding β1 integrins and facilitating proper neutrophil migration toward sites of inflammation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of RGD peptide function and inferred from the rescue of Pecam1-/- neutrophil migration by RGD treatment (Figure 5).

claim: The retention of Pecam1-/- neutrophils in the extravascular interstitium is primarily due to the excessive adhesion of integrins to the components of the extracellular matrix.
source: Therefore, our data strongly suggest that the retention of Pecam1-/- neutrophils in the extravascular interstitium is primarily due to the excessive adhesion of integrins to the components of the extracellular matrix.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking integrin-ECM interactions with RGD peptides rescues the migration defect in Pecam1-/- neutrophils (Figure 5).

claim: Previous studies have proposed that impaired CD31-dependent upregulation of β1-integrin leads to the inability of Pecam1-/- neutrophils to exit blood vessels.
source: Previous studies have proposed that impaired CD31-dependent upregulation of β1-integrin leads to the inability of Pecam1-/- neutrophils to exit blood vessels (Dangerfield et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Dangerfield et al., 2002).

claim: Recent evidence demonstrates that neutrophils lacking β1-integrins actually have an enhanced ability to reach inflamed sites.
source: However, recent evidence challenges this hypothesis by demonstrating that neutrophils lacking β1-integrins actually have an enhanced ability to reach inflamed sites (Sarangi et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous study (Sarangi et al., 2012).

claim: CD31 may be involved in β1-integrin conformation rather than solely regulating its expression.
source: Our present findings suggest that CD31 may be involved in β1-integrin conformation rather than solely regulating its expression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 co-localizes with closed integrins and RGD peptides rescue the migration defect (Figure 2J, Figure 5).

claim: Proteomic analysis revealed that CD31 partners were also associated with the actin cytoskeleton.
source: While our primary focus was on investigating CD31's role in uropod detachment, proteomic analysis revealed that CD31 partners were also associated with the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: Supported by IPA and KEGG pathway analysis showing enrichment of actin cytoskeleton-related proteins in CD31 interactome (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 localizes to the uropod and its absence prevents uropod detachment (Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 4).

evidence: Inferred from the observation that CD31 responds to mechanical stress, localizes to the uropod, and regulates integrin conformation during neutrophil extravasation (Figure 1E, Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 4).
